title: Data-Driven Decision Making in Scholarship Programs: Leveraging Decision Trees and Clustering Algorithms
authors: Espiritu, F. V.; Natividad, M. C. B.; Velasco, R. A.
venue: International Journal in Information Technology in Governance, Education and Business
tldr: Decision trees and K-means clustering applied to 57,342 scholarship applications achieved 80% predictive accuracy and a 31% success rate improvement through an integrated online platform.
problem_and_motivation: The BRO-Ed Scholarship program in Isabela province faces a 541.1% surge in applications, from 5,368 to 34,426 per cycle, overwhelming manual review processes. Subjective and time-consuming evaluation methods risk missing crucial success factors and reducing program effectiveness. There is no systematic, data-driven approach for scholarship application assessment or budget allocation optimization.
approach: Integrated historical scholarship application data from the BRO-Ed program into a unified dataset of 57,342 records after removing 3,100 duplicate entries.
Applied data preprocessing including missing value handling, outlier detection, standardization, normalization, and categorical encoding.
Implemented the C4.5 decision tree algorithm for classification of scholarship application outcomes using information gain ratio.
Applied K-means clustering to group similar applications and identify common characteristics among successful applicants.
Developed an online registration platform using Handlebars.js, Node.js with Express.js, MySQL, and W3.CSS for accessibility.
Evaluated model performance using accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score metrics.
findings: num: Predictive accuracy reached 80% for successful scholarship outcomes and 70% for failure prediction.
num: Online system achieved a 31% higher success rate compared to traditional methods.
num: Dataset completeness improved from 58,892 entries to 57,342 unique entries after duplicate removal.
Academic performance, financial need, and parental occupation were identified as the highest-impact factors for scholarship success.
User satisfaction surveys showed strong preference for the online system due to ease of use and accessibility.
Previous achievements had medium impact on outcomes, while demographic characteristics had low impact.

topics.name: None
topics.justification: Paper addresses educational scholarship management, not personal finance or budget management. The ODIN taxonomy does not contain education-specific topic domains.

topic_relevance.contribution_to_field: This paper contributes to educational data mining by demonstrating how decision trees and clustering algorithms can be integrated with online systems to improve scholarship program management. It provides a practical framework for processing large volumes of scholarship applications using C4.5 and K-means algorithms. The study establishes that data-driven approaches achieve higher accuracy than manual review processes in educational resource allocation. It also contributes a web-based platform architecture for accessibility in educational support programs serving underprivileged communities.
directly_justifies: Decision tree and clustering models achieve 80% predictive accuracy for scholarship outcomes.
Online registration system yields a 31% higher success rate than traditional methods.
Academic performance, financial need, and parental occupation are the strongest predictors of scholarship success.
57,342 unique records were processed after removing 3,100 duplicates from the original dataset.
limits: Study focuses on educational scholarship management rather than personal finance, limiting direct applicability to financial management systems.
Only C4.5 and K-means algorithms were tested, with no comparison to ensemble or deep learning methods.
The dataset is specific to a single scholarship program in one Philippine province, limiting generalizability.
No cross-validation or holdout testing methodology is described for model evaluation.
topic_relevance.topic_mapping_rationale: All topic domains in the ODIN taxonomy were systematically scanned. Domain 6 (Predictive Modeling) was considered but rejected as contextual because the paper applies predictive modeling to educational scholarship data, not personal finance. Domain 12 (Evaluation Frameworks) was considered but rejected as contextual since the evaluation is of a scholarship management system, not a personal finance system. No other domains from the 14-topic taxonomy matched the paper's content on educational data mining, scholarship program management, or web platform development for education. The paper falls entirely outside the personal finance domain, resulting in a 'None' assignment with contextual relevance only.

limitations: Scope limited to a single scholarship program in Isabela province, reducing generalizability to other contexts.
Only C4.5 decision tree and K-means clustering were evaluated, without comparison to modern ensemble or deep learning methods.
No cross-validation or systematic train-test splitting methodology is described for robust model evaluation.
The study does not address real-time processing or scalability for the reported 34,426 annual applications.
Ethical considerations are listed but not empirically evaluated in the results.
